variants: An army, and someone paying for it. Let us not pretend this is about glory. I will make you an offer at the end; you will not like the terms.
So the Barcids' war has found me a new opponent. Understand that I am here for the ledger, not the legend, and ledgers are much harder to kill.
You have won the field. Very well. I have lost cheaper things to worse men. The Council will hear that the Barcids' war lost it, not mine.
Beaten. I shall write it down as an expense and you as a creditor. I pay my creditors. Eventually, and never in full.
There. You are done, and I have lost fewer men than I budgeted for. That is a good day in my trade.
Finished. I shall put your camp in the books as a purchase. Blood is a currency like any other; you simply overpaid.
Steel meets steel. Now the costs begin. I do hope you are keeping accounts, because I am.
My spears are moving. Every one of them is paid through the season, so they will not stop for a little dying.
I am attacking. Do not take it personally; I am simply collecting on ground you owe me.
Forward, in pay order. Mercenaries fight best when they can see the paymaster watching.
You are at my walls. Do you have any idea what those walls cost? Of course not. Nobody who breaks things ever does.
An assault on my camp. Every breach is coming out of someone's wages, and it will not be mine.
You have taken a camp. Take the debts that come with it too; I was rather hoping someone would.
A camp lost. I shall claim it was never mine. That is the beauty of having good clerks.
That camp is mine now. I have already sold the grain in it twice. Do not look so surprised; it is how one makes a profit on war.
Your camp, under new management. I shall keep the wells and fire the garrison. Standard practice.
Your men are dying at a rate that would bankrupt a lesser treasury. I find that admirable and very stupid.
Look at your losses. Whoever is paying for this war is getting very poor value.
My spears are falling. Every one is a contract I have to settle with a widow. Someone will pay for this, and it will not be me.
More of my hired men are coming down the road. Fresh, fed, and paid. You cannot say the same for yours.
Reinforcements. Bought this morning, delivered this afternoon. That is what a treasury is for.
Your commander is dead. A costly man to lose. I have already calculated what it will cost you to replace him; the number is not kind.
So. The Barcids get their wish and I get a spear. Tell the Council the books are in order. They always were.
Nearly bankrupt, then. In men, I mean. I have been bankrupt before; the trick is to owe so much that they cannot afford to finish you.
We are allies, so I am told. I did not vote for it. Keep your men off my supply lines and we shall get along splendidly.
Won. I shall tell the Council it was my doing and yours was very expensive. They will believe half of it.
Lost. I did say this was the Barcids' kind of war. Nobody listens to the man who keeps the books until the books are empty.
My camp is under attack, and my men are paid to fight, not to die. If you want them alive tomorrow, come today.
They are at my walls. Mercenaries have a fine sense of when a paymaster is about to become a corpse. Do hurry.
I am bleeding men, and each one was paid in advance. This is not a battle, it is an audit, and it is going badly.
I am nearly finished. I would rather not be. Consider this an invoice for immediate assistance.
My part is over. I shall be in the Council chamber by morning, explaining how it was your fault. Win anyway.
My spears are marching on them. I do not do this cheaply, so kindly make it count.
I am attacking. Hold your side. If this is wasted, I shall be sending you the bill.
That camp is ours. I have already leased the granary. To you, actually. We can discuss terms.
Your commander is dead. Unfortunate, and expensive. Keep your line; a leaderless ally is a liability I did not agree to insure.
